_readme: MONEY-1379 — a RATIO of two GCP-integration series, grouped, compared to a
ceiling. Used by: pubsub-handler-failure and gemini-token-quota.
The calling script passes FULLY-FORMED numerator and denominator expressions
(`num` / `den`), so this template knows nothing about metrics, scopes or
group-bys — one of the two numerators is a two-term sum, which no
metric/scope/suffix parameterisation could have expressed. The grouping
lives inside those expressions; both sides must group by the SAME tag or
Datadog divides one group's numerator by another's denominator.
TWO OMISSIONS THAT ARE DECISIONS, recorded here because each looks like a
gap otherwise:
1. `remote_server_4xx` IS DELIBERATELY NOT IN THE FAILURE NUMERATOR. It is
not an upstream error and it is not a handler throwing — it is OUR OWN
`pubsubDedupeMiddleware` (workers/src/lib/pubsub-dedupe.ts) answering
409 RETRY_LATER to a redelivery whose claim is still live. That is the
dedupe working exactly as designed: the first copy is still running and
will succeed. Counting it as a failure would make every slow handler
report a failure rate climbing toward 1.0 while losing no work at all.
The numerator is `remote_server_5xx + unreachable` — the route throwing,
and the service down or timing out.
2. THERE IS NO MONITOR OVER THE GEMINI *REQUESTS* QUOTA. Measured
2026-09-11, the `.limit` of
`gcp.generativelanguage.quota.generate_content_paid_tier_3_requests`
reads 9223372036854775807 — INT64_MAX, i.e. unlimited — for both
models. `usage / limit` against that can never cross any
threshold, so the monitor would be green forever and indistinguishable
from a healthy one: the MONEY-1238 defect class, shipped on purpose.
The TOKEN quota (`…_input_token_count.limit` = 20,000,000 tokens/min) is
the real ceiling, and that is the ratio this template is used for.
name: [{{env}}] {{label}}
_managed_tag_rationale: `managed-by:apply-perf-monitors` is its OWN namespace, distinct from the
apply-service-monitors.sh share. Reusing theirs would put these rows in
both scripts' listings, where each prunes what it does not recognise.
